entities.summary:
Lucius Sempronius Atratinus (born 72 BCE, died 7 CE) was a Roman politician and orator whose career spanned the tumultuous final decades of the Roman Republic and the nascent years of the Augustan Principate. A member of the ancient patrician Sempronia gens, he achieved the suffect consulship in 34 BCE, a critical period during the Second Triumvirate's power struggles following the assassination of Julius Caesar. His early career is notably illuminated by his role as prosecutor in the infamous trial of Marcus Caelius Rufus in 56 BCE, a legal battle that provided the backdrop for Cicero's celebrated speech, *Pro Caelio*, thereby securing Atratinus a lasting, albeit secondary, place in the annals of Roman legal and literary history.

Atratinus's public life commenced with his unsuccessful prosecution of Marcus Caelius Rufus in 56 BCE, a case brought on charges including *vis* (public violence) and poisoning. Despite Caelius's acquittal, Atratinus's participation as a young, ambitious orator, alongside the elder Lucius Herennius Balbus and Publius Clodius Pulcher, marked his entry into the Roman political arena. He subsequently served as quaestor in 47 BCE under Marcus Antonius in Greece, and later as curule aedile in 40 BCE. His political ascent culminated in 34 BCE when, as a loyal supporter of Antonius, he was appointed suffect consul, replacing Lucius Scribonius Libo. This appointment placed him at the heart of state administration during the escalating tensions between Antonius and Octavian, just prior to the final civil war.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Lucius Sempronius Atratinus is significant for his role as a suffect consul during the turbulent Second Triumvirate, representing the political fluidity of the era, and for his lasting, albeit indirect, contribution to Roman literature through Cicero's *Pro Caelio*.
